generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, an exam under time pressure is where prepared knowledge either reaches the page or does not. Arriving settled and reading the whole paper first stop you pouring everything you know about a keyword onto the page instead of answering the question set. Dividing your time by the marks, and planning a brief answer before writing, protect the considered responses that earn the most credit.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students, equally well prepared, sitting the same two-hour exam with two equally weighted questions.

Student A arrives just in time and hurries to the desk, flustered. With one pen and no watch, they scan the paper, spot the first familiar keyword, and write down everything connected to it. That answer runs well over an hour, so the second question is rushed and half planned. The knowledge was there; the strategy let it leak away.

Student B arrives early, lays out two pens and a watch, and reads both questions before choosing. Seeing that they carry equal marks, Student B gives each one an hour, spends ten minutes planning an argument, and writes to that plan. When time runs short on the second answer, they close it with a brief conclusion rather than leave it unfinished. The preparation showed because the time was controlled.

Both knew the material. Only Student B protected that knowledge with timing and a calm start, and so turned it into a complete paper.
generatedProse.summary: Exam-day strategy is how prepared knowledge becomes marks. You can now explain how an organised approach manages anxiety and protects performance, analyse contrasting approaches to find the decisions that matter, and devise a timed plan for an exam of your own. With active revision behind you and a clear plan for the day, your preparation has the best chance to show.

check.body: In the worked example, which decision most clearly cost Student A marks?

items.text: Spending well over an hour on the first answer, which left the second rushed.
Arriving a few minutes before the start.
Spotting a familiar keyword in the first question.
Bringing only one pen to the exam.

feedback.correct: That's right. Letting the first answer run well over an hour left too little time for the second.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the decision about how Student A spent the time across the two answers.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The clearest cost was spending well over an hour on the first answer, which left the second rushed. The late arrival and single pen added stress but did not directly lose the marks.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
